_note: Kid-safe fact sheet per place id (places.json). Only facts we are confident in; each carries a source. 'estimated': true marks crew-proposed names whose size/position are estimates, not IAU values. 'numbers' lists every number the guide may say about the place (checked within +-10%).

facts.text: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed here on July 20, 1969, on Apollo 11.
The Sea of Tranquility is about 873 km across.
It isn't water: the dark 'seas' are old lava that cooled flat.
The astronauts' footprints are still there, because there is no wind on the Moon.
The plateau is about 200 km across and rises above the lava plains around it.
Aristarchus crater, on its edge, is about 40 km wide and the brightest big crater on the side we see.
The plateau is covered in dark volcanic glass beads sprayed out long ago.
Orientale is a bullseye of rings about 930 km wide, made by a giant impact.
It has three main rings, like ripples in a pond that froze.
It sits on the Moon's western edge, so from Earth we only see its side.
It formed about 3.8 billion years ago.
Hertzsprung is a huge ringed basin, more than 500 km wide.
It is on the far side, which never faces Earth.
Vavilov is a far-side crater about 98 km wide.
It sits on the edge of the giant Hertzsprung basin.
Ohm is a far-side crater about 64 km wide.
It is young, so its bright rays haven't faded yet.
Glushko is about 43 km wide, near the Moon's western edge.
It is a young crater with long bright rays.
Reiner Gamma is a bright swirl about 70 km long, shaped like a tadpole.
It sits where the Moon's rocks have a little magnetic field.
It is on the side we see, in a big dark lava plain.
The Artemis II crew proposed naming this crater Integrity, after their Orion spacecraft.
The crew said it lies halfway between Orientale and Ohm. Its size and spot here are estimates.
facts.source: NASA Artemis II mission audio (position estimated)

facts.text: The Artemis II crew proposed the name Carroll for a bright spot, to remember someone from their astronaut family.
The crew said it is northwest of Glushko. Its size and spot here are estimates.
facts.source: NASA Artemis II mission audio (position estimated)

facts.text: Tycho is about 85 km wide.
Its bright rays stretch more than 1,500 km across the Moon.
It is young for a Moon crater, about 100 million years old.
It has a mountain in the middle, about 2 km tall.
Copernicus is about 93 km wide and nearly 4 km deep.
facts.source: IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature / NASA LRO

facts.text: It has stair-step walls and mountains in the middle.
It is about 800 million years old.
The Sea of Rains, Mare Imbrium, is about 1,146 km across.
It is a giant impact basin later filled with dark lava.
Apollo 15 astronauts landed at its eastern edge in 1971.
The Sea of Crises is about 556 km across.
It is a round dark patch you can see with just your eyes.
The Luna 24 robot brought soil home from here in 1976.
Shackleton is a crater about 21 km wide at the Moon's south pole.
Its floor never gets sunlight, so it is super cold and may hold ice.
It is about 4 km deep.
Artemis astronauts plan to land in the south pole region.
Tsiolkovskiy is a far-side crater about 185 km wide.
Its floor is filled with dark lava, with a bright mountain in the middle.
It was first seen in 1959 in photos from the Luna 3 spacecraft.
It is about 2,500 km across, one of the biggest impact craters in the solar system.
It is the biggest and oldest known basin on the Moon.
It is about 8 km deep in places.
